stories.title: Height Differences in Bombay Trains
stories.description: Amit recalls observing in the 1990s that passengers in the first-class compartments of Bombay local trains were significantly taller than those in second-class, a visceral illustration of how nutrition and social class impact physical (and cognitive) development.

stories.title: The Beautiful Tree Paradox
stories.description: Ajay discusses James Tooley's research in Hyderabad slums, which revealed that poor parents often chose to pay for budget private schools rather than send their children to free government schools, effectively 'voting with their feet' for accountability.

stories.title: Josh Felman on Jewish Success
stories.description: Ajay shares an insight from Josh Felman about why the Jewish community has such high intellectual achievement. Beyond the 'portable human capital' theory, Felman pointed to the tradition of ordinary people (not just priests) giving 10-15 minute orations integrating religious texts with daily life, fostering deep intellectual capability.

stories.title: The Bias for Action Debate
stories.description: Amit and Ajay have a friendly disagreement about 'bias for action'. Amit argues it is essential for creators (learning by doing), while Ajay argues it is dangerous for the state (which wields coercive power and should act slowly and rigorously).

stories.title: Rahul Dravid in the Office
stories.description: Ajay recounts playing office cricket with Rahul Dravid using a 'squeezy ball'. After Ajay bowled a wide and then clean bowled Dravid twice, Dravid jokingly said, 'Fuck you, Shoaib Akhtar, I'm not playing with you' and threw the bat.

recommendations.comment: Karthik Muralidharan's book, which contains a detailed chapter on the state of education in India.
James Tooley's book on budget private schools and how the poor are educating themselves.

recommendations.item: The Collected Stories of Lydia Davis
recommendations.comment: Amit recommends this collection of short stories to enter the minds of others and enrich one's own life through osmosis.

recommendations.item: The Collected Essays of Lydia Davis
recommendations.comment: Amit recommends her essays for insights into writing and literature.
Ajay recommends Harper Lee's classic, noting it's even more relevant now as it shows that 'history never ended' and darkness still exists.

recommendations.item: The Seen and the Unseen Ep. 301
recommendations.comment: Amit recommends the episode with Natasha Badhwar for deep insights on parenting and education.
Amit praises their 'Tank Scrub' sessions where members present on what they learned that week, fostering multidisciplinary learning.

core_ideas.description: Contary to popular belief, education (measured by years of schooling) does not necessarily cause economic development. Often, development leads to more education, not the other way around (Lant Pritchett's 'Where Has All the Education Gone?').
Education often functions as a signaling mechanism (like a Louis Vuitton bag) to sort people for the labor market rather than actually building human capital.
The current education system is a 19th-century industrial machine designed to produce conscientious, obedient workers, not to foster flexible general intelligence or 'learning how to learn'.
James Heckman's work shows that the most high-leverage investment is in early childhood (0-5 years), where the home environment and 'overhearing' complex conversations matter immensely.

Instead of funding schools (which leads to inefficiency), the state should fund students via vouchers, allowing parents (who have the best incentives) to choose the best school, fostering competition.

It is unfair for the state to spend ~₹10,000/child in government schools while giving zero support to poor parents who choose private schools. Spending should be equalized per child, regardless of school choice.
A 'bias for action' is virtuous for individuals and creators (learning by doing) but dangerous for the state (which should deliberate carefully before using coercive power).

jokes_and_cultural_references.context: A reference to the idea that India's population should be viewed as a resource of minds, not just mouths to feed.
Ajay uses this as a metaphor for the signaling value of elite degrees—expensive status symbols that prove you could afford them.
Ajay quotes an old Unix fortune: 'School is a daycare for teenagers'.
Ajay warns against believing that credentials (like IIT degrees) inherently make you superior or knowledgeable.
A callback to the previous episode's joke about not needing to be a hen to know about eggs.
